findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Internal Audit Annual Report and Fraud Log
findings.headline: S106 developer contribution monitoring process undergoing comprehensive external overhaul and consultant review
findings.detail: The council appointed an external consultant to conduct a full review of the s106 monitoring arrangement, including review of all open s106 agreements, balances, and processes. Internal audit's planned audit was postponed. The consultant is undertaking day-to-day s106 monitoring tasks while process mapping, legal records review, and system development work continues. The work is described as ongoing with multiple workstreams still in progress.
findings.matters: S106 contributions are a material income stream for councils and represent contractual obligations. A comprehensive process overhaul indicates the prior arrangement had issues requiring external intervention that could affect income certainty or legal compliance.
findings.figures: External consultant engaged on full s106 review; multiple ongoing workstreams on process mapping, legal records, and systems
findings.quote: However, it was requested that the audit be postponed as the Council had appointed an external consultant to review the s106 monitoring arrangement in full, which included a review of all open s106 agreements and balances and a review of processes and procedures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Internal Audit Annual Report and Fraud Log
findings.headline: Stockyard Project (major town centre capital scheme) audit delayed, with no assurance yet given on project controls
findings.detail: The audit of the Stockyard Project was postponed at management request and remains ongoing at the time of reporting. The project does not yet have an internal audit opinion on the adequacy and effectiveness of its management and control framework. Stockyard is a significant capital initiative under the Sustainable Growth and Infrastructure theme.
findings.matters: A major capital project operating without internal audit assurance creates governance and control risk. Lenders need confidence that significant capital schemes have been properly audited and that project controls are operating effectively.
findings.figures: Stockyard Project audit ongoing; no assurance opinion issued
findings.quote: The audit of the Stockyard Project was delayed at management request until the first quarter of 2026/27 and remains ongoing at the time of reporting – as such, assurances have not yet been given on the management of this project.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Internal Audit Annual Report and Fraud Log
findings.headline: Monthly bank reconciliation control lapsed due to staffing vacancy and turnover in the finance team
findings.detail: Monthly General Bank Account reconciliations were not up to date at the time of the internal audit due to a changeover in staff and a vacancy within the finance team. Weekly reconciliations between bank statement and cash book were completed as a compensating control, but the delay in the core monthly control indicates resourcing or continuity issues in the critical finance function.
findings.matters: Staffing instability in the finance team creates risk of control lapses and suggests the team may be under-resourced for its current workload, which could affect the timeliness and reliability of financial reporting.
findings.figures: Monthly reconciliations not current at audit; weekly reconciliations completed throughout period
findings.quote: However, due to a changeover in staff and a vacancy within the team, the monthly General Bank Account reconciliations were not up to date at the time of the audit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Internal Audit Annual Report and Fraud Log
findings.headline: Implementation of audit recommendations has slowed, with 26% of agreed actions over 3 months overdue including one High priority item
findings.detail: Only 69% of the 65 agreed management actions due in 2025/26 were implemented during the year, down from 80% in 2024/25. More concerning, 17 actions (26% of total) are now overdue by more than 3 months, including 1 high-priority action. This indicates management is not following through on audit remediation timescales at the expected pace.
findings.matters: Slow or incomplete implementation of audit recommendations indicates either management capacity constraints or deprioritisation of control improvements, leaving identified weaknesses unresolved and increasing operational risk.
findings.figures: 69% implementation rate (2025/26) vs 80% (2024/25); 17 actions (26%) overdue over 3 months; 1 High priority action overdue
findings.quote: Of the agreed management actions due for implementation during 2025/26, 69% had been completed during the year. This is a reduction on the previous year (i.e. 80% implementation in 2024/25).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Internal Audit Annual Report and Fraud Log
findings.headline: Council's control environment given Moderate Assurance, indicating gaps in controls that pose medium risk to delivery of objectives
findings.detail: The Chief Internal Auditor's opinion is Moderate Assurance for the adequacy and effectiveness of the Council's control environment in 2025/26. This is the overall opinion covering the system of internal control, governance arrangements and risk management. Moderate Assurance means there are gaps in the internal control framework which pose a medium risk to delivery of the council's objectives.
findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk would be concerned that the authority's control framework has identified gaps creating medium-risk exposure that could affect financial management and service delivery.
findings.figures: Moderate Assurance opinion (2025/26)
findings.quote: It is my opinion that Moderate Assurance can be given over the adequacy and effectiveness of the Council's control environment for 2025/26

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End 2025/26
findings.headline: Government-mandated food waste collection service identified as key driver of future financial deficits
findings.detail: The medium-term forecast deficits are explicitly attributed to 'the introduction of a food waste collection service as required by government'. A £820k food waste vehicle budget was completely unspent in 2025/26 and carried forward, signalling project delays or phasing.
findings.matters: Mandated services create fixed costs with no discretionary removal option. If government is not funding the cost, this creates permanent budget pressure with no policy solution.
findings.figures: Food waste vehicle budget £820k unspent in 2025/26
findings.quote: This is due to the implications of the Governments funding review coupled with the impact of the introduction of a food waste collection service as required by government.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End 2025/26
findings.headline: Special Expenses working balance remains below council-approved target; reserves described as 'too low'
findings.detail: The Special Expenses working balance stayed at £50k and could not be increased to the approved target of £100k. The paper states the current level is 'too low compared to the level of variances that has been seen in recent years' and 'will need to be kept under review'.
findings.matters: A working balance below prudent levels for historical variances is a weak financial buffer. Future adverse variances could force rapid drawdowns or service cuts.
findings.figures: Current £50k vs target £100k; underfunded by £50k
findings.quote: The Special Expenses Working Balance remains the same at £50k and has not been able to be increased, with there being no underspend, to the new target level approved by Council to £100k.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End 2025/26
findings.headline: Homelessness spending driven by increased demand for emergency bed and breakfast accommodation
findings.detail: Homelessness budget overspent by £95k in 2025/26, with the paper citing increased spend on B&B accommodation due to demand. The phrasing ('mainly relating to increased spend on... due to demand') suggests ongoing pressure rather than a one-off.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends signal underlying social stress or demographic change. If homelessness demand is rising, this is both a forward cost exposure and a signal of stress in the area.
findings.figures: £95k overspend; no trend data given
findings.quote: Homelessness (£95k) Mainly relating to increased spend on Bed & Breakfast accommodation due to demand.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End 2025/26
findings.headline: Finance team turnover means interim staff closed 2025/26 accounts; post-closedown errors are expected
findings.detail: The council experienced significant accountancy staff turnover and is filling vacancies with interim staff. Accounts were closed by interim staff not involved in budget setting or year-round monitoring, creating continuity gaps. The report explicitly flags that 'it is likely that this will result in a number of post closedown adjustments to correct any errors'.
findings.matters: If financial statements require post-publication correction, audit confidence weakens and account reliability is questioned. This is a material governance risk.
findings.figures: No quantified impact yet; described as likely but uncertain
findings.quote: The Council has seen a significant turnover in accountancy staff in the past few months and is currently carrying a number of vacancies which are being filled by interims. This has meant the accounts have had to be closed by largely interim staff who were not involved in the original budget setting or monitoring throughout the year. This has caused some issues in terms of continuity, and it is likely that this will result in a number of post closedown adjustments to correct any errors identified during the audit

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End 2025/26
findings.headline: Medium-term forecasts show increasing deficits that cannot be met from reserves
findings.detail: The MTFS approved in February 2026 forecasts increasing deficits over the next three years that are too large to be funded from reserves. The deficits are driven by the government funding review and the mandated introduction of a food waste collection service. No funding solution is described.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has a credible plan to close forecast deficits. If reserves cannot fund them and no solutions are yet in place, this signals medium-term financial stress.
findings.figures: Specific deficit figures not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: The Council's medium term financial strategy approved in February 2026 when the budget for 2025-26 was approved provides forward forecasts for the next 3 financial year. This show increasing forecast deficits in future years that are to high to be met from reserves.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End for 2025/26
findings.headline: Rent income shortfall of £28k from high void levels, plus £13k from delayed/reduced Independent Living Charge
findings.detail: Rent income underperformed by £28k due to the high void numbers (195 vs 150). Additionally, the Independent Living Charge was delayed to week 3 of the year and applied at a lower amount than approved, generating a £13k shortfall. The council notes 'a sharp focus on income recovery' is underway, but also flags risks from economic hardship and welfare reform affecting collection.
findings.matters: Income shortfalls compound overspend problems and reduce the HRA's financial headroom. Tenant economic stress and welfare changes are cyclical risks that may worsen if recession deepens.
findings.figures: Rent income shortfall £28k (voids); Independent Living Charge shortfall £13k; Heating charges reduction £20k
findings.quote: The high voids referred to in 5.1.5 above has also had a knock on impact to the income from rents, a shortfall of £28k was therefore the final year end position.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End for 2025/26
findings.headline: Decent Homes Standard 2 and Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard coming in 2026 will likely require significant changes to investment plans and service standards
findings.detail: The council flags that new regulatory requirements (Decent Homes 2 and MEES) are being introduced in 2026. These 'additional pressures on the HRA need to be considered' and the report states 'it is likely that significant changes will need to be made to planned investment, service standards, resources and the range of services provided'. Modelling is underway but not yet complete.
findings.matters: Regulatory changes drive unbudgeted capex and revenue spend. The council is already unaffordable and squeezed; adding regulatory obligations without visible funding creates cliff risk. A lender needs to know what the final cost and timeline for DHS2 compliance will be.
findings.figures: New requirements introduced 2026; modelling to be completed for 2027-28 budget setting
findings.quote: New requirements have been introduced in 2026 around the new Decent Homes Standard and the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard. These additional pressures on the HRA need to be considered as part of the review for 2027/28 budgets. It is likely that significant changes will need to be made to planned investment, service standards, resources and the range of services provided to maintain a sustainable HRA.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End for 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 53% of budget; major projects delayed or awaiting planning permission
findings.detail: The HRA spent £4.296m of £8.096m capital budget (47% underspend). Major delays include: Fairmead Community Centre conversion (£362k carry-forward, awaiting planning permission), Douglas Jane conversion (£90k, awaiting planning), Energy Efficiency programme (£1.52m underspent, procurement delayed), and multiple lift and rewiring projects delayed by procurement or tenant refusals.
findings.matters: Poor capital delivery suggests project management or procurement weakness. Extended delays accumulate costs and defer the council's ability to meet regulatory standards (fire safety, damp, energy efficiency). Planning delays on major regeneration projects indicate external constraints.
findings.figures: Capital outturn £4,296k of £8,096k budget; £2,483k carried forward; Energy Efficiency £1.52m underspent
findings.quote: In relation to the HRA capital programme against the budget of £8,096k, the provisional outturn is £4,296k resulting in an underspend of £3,799k, of which £2,483k is to be carried forward into 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End for 2025/26
findings.headline: Regeneration Reserve depleted by revenue overspend, significantly reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: The council used its Regeneration & Development Reserve to cover the £678k revenue overspend. The report explicitly warns that 'this reduces the flexibility in future years to fund any further overspends or meet unexpected costs and significantly reduces financial flexibility'. The reserve falls from £2.029m budgeted to £1.003m actual by year-end, and is projected to fall further to £56k by 2026-27.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion reduces the council's capacity to absorb future shocks or invest in non-routine items. If reserves fall below policy minimum, the council would face forced service cuts or external intervention.
findings.figures: Regeneration Reserve: £2.029m budgeted → £1.003m actual 2025-26 → £56k estimated 2026-27
findings.quote: The use of the Regeneration & Development Reserve for the revenue overspend has caused the in-year depletion of its balance. This reduces the flexibility in future years to fund any further overspends or meet unexpected costs and significantly reduces financial flexibility.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End for 2025/26
findings.headline: Interest cover ratio of 0.34 means the HRA cannot service its debt from operating income; borrowing is unaffordable
findings.detail: The HRA's interest cover ratio collapsed to 0.34 in 2025-26 (ideal range 1.10-1.25 nationally), meaning the account only covered 34% of annual debt service from its own resources. The report explicitly states that borrowing for housing development or stock maintenance is currently unaffordable. This blocks capital investment unless funded from reserves or receipts.
findings.matters: This is a hard constraint on the council's ability to invest in new housing or maintain the existing stock. Any lender considering financing the HRA needs to understand that the operating model cannot currently support additional debt.
findings.figures: Interest Cover 2025-26: 0.34 (vs ideal 1.10-1.25); Margin 3.07% (vs national average 22%)
findings.quote: In 2025-26 the account was unable to service its full amount debt from its annual resource (just 34%), and reserves were required to make the remainder of this payment.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revenue and Capital Budget Provisional Year End for 2025/26
findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £678k drawing down reserves unsustainably
findings.detail: The HRA delivered an overspend of £678k against approved budget, with the council drawing £598k from reserves at year-end. The report notes that three-year overspends have totalled £1.167m and that 'future overspends are therefore not sustainable at current levels'. The Regeneration & Development Reserve has been materially depleted to cover the revenue shortfall.
findings.matters: Recurring overspends eating into reserves indicate structural imbalance in the HRA and reduce financial flexibility to handle shocks or new requirements. A lender would be concerned about the council's ability to sustain housing investment.
findings.figures: £678k overspend vs approved budget; £598,516 deficit at Net Operating Expenditure; £1.167m cumulative overspend 2024-2026
findings.quote: Future overspends are therefore not sustainable at current levels, overspends over the period 2024-2026 have totalled £1.167m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revenue Budget Proposals 2026/27 for Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: HRA borrowing of £31m with £2m loans maturing in 2026/27; refinancing strategy depends on interest rate falls
findings.detail: The council has total HRA borrowing of around £31m, with £2m of loans maturing in 2026/27. Treasury advice is to defer refinancing pending expected interest rate falls, rather than refinance at current rates. This strategy carries risk if rate expectations do not materialise.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk and interest rate exposure; the strategy assumes rate falls that are not guaranteed, and if rates remain high or rise further, refinancing costs will be higher than planned.
findings.figures: £31m total HRA borrowing; £2m maturing in 2026/27
findings.quote: The Councils HRA borrowing will be around £31m at 31 March 2026, within which there are £2m of maturing loans to consider in 2026/27, the advice from our treasury management team is that interest rates are expected to fall in the future, and it would be beneficial to wait to re-borrow until rates fall to lower levels.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revenue Budget Proposals 2026/27 for Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Rent arrears showing improvement but council explicitly acknowledges continuing risk to income collection
findings.detail: Rent arrears have improved from 7.48% (2024-25 year-end) to 4.87% (2025-26 year-end) to 3.59% (January 2026). However, the council explicitly states in the risk section that it 'carries risk relating to rent arrears performance and continued focus is necessary', indicating improvement is not yet secure.
findings.matters: Rent is the HRA's primary income source. Arrears volatility directly affects cash flow and ability to service debt; the council's own language indicates this remains a fragile position.
findings.quote: This positive progress is welcome, but the Council still carries risk relating to rent arrears performance and continued focus is necessary.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revenue Budget Proposals 2026/27 for Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Major Repairs Reserve declining sharply from £2.17m to £1.31m in coming year, reducing investment flexibility
findings.detail: The Major Repairs Reserve, which funds planned maintenance and investment in the housing stock, is forecast to fall by £866k in 2026-27 and continues declining to £515k by 2028. This reduces the council's capacity to respond to unexpected capital needs or stock condition issues.
findings.matters: This reserve is essential for maintaining stock quality (the council has a target of 96% decent homes by 2028). Depletion limits investment flexibility and may constrain future capital programmes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revenue Budget Proposals 2026/27 for Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Interest coverage ratio of 1.22x in 2026/27 shows HRA business plan only just becoming sustainable after years uncovered
findings.detail: The HRA was not covering interest costs on borrowing in 2024/25 and 2025/26. It becomes covered for the first time in 2026/27 at 1.22x (meaning operating surplus covers interest only 1.22 times), but then deteriorates to 1.13x in 2027/28. This marginal coverage leaves little headroom for cost pressures or income shortfalls.
findings.matters: Interest coverage is a key metric for HRA financial sustainability. A ratio below ~1.5x indicates a business plan under stress with limited capacity to absorb additional borrowing or cost escalation.
findings.quote: This indicator for 2026-27 shows: [table with] Interest Cover 1.22 [for 2026/27]

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revenue Budget Proposals 2026/27 for Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: New damp and mould emergency regulations creating £191k overspend in current year with expected continuation
findings.detail: New legislation on damp and mould emergency hazards has substantially increased demand for works outside the standard repairs contract. The council estimates £191k overspend in 2025-26 alone from this regulatory pressure, with early indications suggesting the demand will persist.
findings.matters: This is a continuing regulatory cost that will persist into future years and potentially reduce the benefit of any savings achieved through repairs contract reprocurement.
findings.figures: £191k overspend estimated
findings.quote: Works outside of PPP (Price Per Property) are expected to increase substantially following the introduction of new regulations regarding emergency hazards damp and mould where we are expecting increased demand and high spend. Early indications of increased demand are being used to estimate the overall impact, and a year-end estimate is currently £191k overspend.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revenue Budget Proposals 2026/27 for Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Void property costs escalating sharply (£400k overspend) and forcing contract reprocurement after value-for-money review
findings.detail: Void volumes (189+ forecast) far exceed the budgeted 150 per year. Average void cost has risen from budgeted £3.5k to £4k in reality. A value-for-money review found the current repairs and voids contract uneconomic and the council is now reprocuring with a different payment model. This represents a structural cost pressure that has driven management action.
findings.matters: This shows sector-wide cost pressures (repairs costs up 55% on pre-pandemic) are hitting this council acutely, and even after contract reprocurement, sustainability depends on new contract delivering better value.
findings.figures: 150 voids budgeted, 189+ forecast; £3.5k to £4k average cost increase; £400k estimated overspend
findings.quote: The number of voids budgeted for in the year was 150, which is historically the average number per year. However, 139 have already become void this year to date, and there is an expectation of a further 50+ this year... The expected overspend on this is estimated at £400k... Earlier in 2025 a value for money review was completed which showed that the current voids contract does not represent value for money, leading to a decision to re-procure the contract with a different payment model.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revenue Budget Proposals 2026/27 for Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £1.007m in current year (2025-26) drives down reserves despite maintaining £1m working balance target
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £1.007m overspend in 2025-26, comprising £961k expenditure overspend and £46k income reduction. This overspend is being funded by drawing down the contribution to reserves, meaning the reserve transfer is reduced from the planned £329k to a transfer-out of £594k, while the working balance itself remains at £1m. This reflects significant budget pressures that are being contained only through reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion reduces financial resilience to absorb future shocks or cost pressures in a service where the council has a statutory duty to avoid deficit.
findings.figures: £1.007m overspend; £961k expenditure overspend; £46k income shortfall; reserve contribution reduces from £329k contribution to £594k draw-out
findings.quote: At 30 November 2025 the Net Cost of Services shows an estimated year end position of a £1.007m overspend; this is partly offset by the expected increase in interest on investment balances of £84k. The £923k remaining overspend will increase the transfer from the reserve in order to maintain the £1m working balance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Decent Homes Standard update expected in coming years; council cannot properly plan long-term investment for housing stock
findings.detail: Council has achieved 96% compliance and plans to reach 100% by 2028, but anticipates the regulatory standard itself will be updated. Until the new requirements are announced and costings understood, the council cannot plan beyond 2028; future investment levels are unknown and may be material.
findings.matters: Unfunded regulatory liability lurking ahead; council will face sudden capital demand shock when new standard is announced, with no time to plan funding
findings.figures: 96% decent homes achieved; 100% target by 2028
findings.quote: The Council will keep a close eye on future changes to the Decent Homes Standard and will update its investment plans accordingly, particularly as changes to the decent homes standard are expected to be announced in the coming years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation decision pending; council submitted unitary proposal to Government in November 2025
findings.detail: As part of government devolution plans, Melton submitted proposals (interim in March 2025, final in November 2025) to move from two-tier to unitary local government. Outcome will fundamentally alter council's structure, financial arrangements, and capabilities. Until decided, medium-term planning is constrained.
findings.matters: Structural uncertainty ahead prevents coherent medium-term financial and capital planning; potential impact on staffing, systems, and debt arrangements depending on reorganisation outcome
findings.figures: Interim proposal submitted 21 March 2025; final proposal submitted end November 2025
findings.quote: The Council alongside all districts in Leicestershire and Rutland County Council submitted our interim plans on the 21 March 2025 setting out how our proposals meet the needs of our local communities. Our final proposal was submitted to Government at the end of November 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Lake Terrace drainage project described as complex, longstanding and high-risk; additional £260k required beyond original allocation
findings.detail: This surface water drainage project is a critical but problematic asset issue. The council acknowledges it carries 'a high degree of risk' and will require £260k more than originally budgeted. The complexity and history suggest risk of further cost escalation or timeline delay, with oversight now escalated to Property and Assets Programme Board.
findings.matters: High-risk capital project with unresolved complexity signals potential for cost overruns and delays; indicates asset management challenges in identifying and scoping problems
findings.figures: £260,000 additional capital required
findings.quote: This is a complex and longstanding issue, and the project must progress to ensure that surface water is channelled correctly into the appropriate drainage system... Given the scale and complexity of the work, the project carries a high degree of risk and will be overseen through the Property and Assets Programme Board. It is currently anticipated that an additional £260,000 will be required within the capital programme to enable the project to proceed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Working-age population declining 4% while council ages; threatens tax base and increases service demand
findings.detail: Melton's population grew only 2.8% versus England's 6.6%. More concerning: the working-age population (15-64) fell 4.0% while over-65s grew 29.6%. The council ranked 305th out of 309 English authorities for total population. This demographic shift reduces the tax base while increasing demand for elderly services.
findings.matters: Declining working-age population shrinks council tax base while aging profile increases service demand and capital needs (adaptations, healthcare facilities, burial capacity); narrows financial headroom
findings.figures: Working-age population down 4.0%; over-65s up 29.6%; total growth only 2.8%
findings.quote: In Melton, there has been an increase of 29.6% in people aged 65 years and over, a decrease of 4.0% in people aged 15 to 64 years, and a decrease of 3.6% in children aged under 15 years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council will need to borrow on General Fund for first time; capital receipts reserve will drop to £154k by end 2026/27
findings.detail: Current capital receipts balance forecast to fall to £154k after £499k expenditure in 2026/27, leaving almost nothing for future schemes. The document explicitly states this will likely trigger borrowing on the General Fund, which is currently debt-free. As the council's own asset base available for disposal is limited, capital receipts cannot be relied upon for future funding.
findings.matters: A currently debt-free council shifting to borrower status is a material change in financial structure; debt serviceability becomes an issue for lenders and the council's financial trajectory
findings.figures: £154k balance forecast 2026/27; £499k planned expenditure; £1.5m borrowing assumed in current plan
findings.quote: Therefore, once the future capital programme becomes more developed the future funding requirements will need to be reviewed which may lead to a borrowing requirement on the general fund which is currently debt free.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: No contingency reserve has been set aside in 2026/27 budget 'due to affordability'; S151 Officer's statement of adequacy is qualified to exclude food waste costs.
findings.detail: The budget contains "no contingency" for 2026/27 due to affordability constraints. This increases operational risk. The S151 Officer's statement on the adequacy of reserves is explicitly qualified: "the Council has adequate reserves for its immediate and short term needs based on the budget proposals excluding the costs of a food waste collection service. However, should the future year deficits as set out in the MTFS be realised and an exemption cannot be secured for the delivery of a food waste collection service then service reductions will have to be considered". This is a material qualification.
findings.matters: A lender will note the absence of contingency reserve and the qualified statement from the S151 Officer. This indicates the council has no buffer for unexpected events and the finance officer is expressing concern about medium-term sustainability.
findings.figures: No contingency included 2026/27. Corporate Priorities Reserve forecast to be exhausted 2029/30 (or 2028/29 with food waste).
findings.quote: No contingency has been included in the budget for 2026/27 due to affordability.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Finance settlement violates New Burdens Doctrine by subsuming food waste funding into overall allocation without transparency; funding shortfall is described as 'a source of significant frustration across the sector'.
findings.detail: Government previously committed to fully fund food waste collections under the New Burdens Doctrine, requiring central government to fully meet additional costs of new responsibilities. However, funding has been subsumed within overall settlement "so it is unclear how much has been allocated to support food waste collection services across the borough". The report describes this as "a source of significant frustration across the sector and represents a key financial risk for this Council". Council recommendations note the Council's "dissatisfaction with the shortfall in funding provided" and notes that "other Councils have advised DEFRA of their intention and need to delay implementation of food waste based on their specific circumstances".
findings.matters: A lender assesses governance risk. This signals a breach of funding principle and sector-wide dispute with government. Other councils are in similar position, indicating systemic risk across English local government.
findings.figures: Full food waste cost: £779,380 + £112,370 annual vehicle replacement. New burdens funding subsumed and non-transparent within settlement.
findings.quote: The Government had previously committed to fully meet any new burdens arising from implementing food waste collections. This commitment would be in line with the New Burdens Doctrine, a principle requiring central government to fully fund the additional costs of new responsibilities or policies imposed on local authorities and therefore preventing an unfunded strain on budgets. However, contrary to this, the allocation of funding has been subsumed within the overall settlement and so it is unclear how much has been allocated to support food waste collection services across the borough.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Special Expenses Melton Mowbray reserves heavily depleted; cemetery capacity exhausted in 4-26 years with new cemetery being cost prohibitive.
findings.detail: Special Expenses reserves have been "heavily depleted in recent years as a result of previous deficits". Current working balance is £50k, proposed to increase to £100k. Cemetery capacity analysis shows burial plots exhausted in ~10 years (with improvements, 16 years); cremation plots in 4 years (with improvements, 30 years). A new cemetery is rated as Very High/Critical risk: "cost prohibitive for Special Expenses in terms of both revenue and capital including the costs to maintain the closed churchyard". Frisby closed churchyard repairs identified additional urgent works in 2025/26 (£7k) that increase 2026/27 deficit on that fund.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand long-term capital and revenue obligations. Cemetery service is statutory and must be provided; cost-prohibitive solutions signal medium-term funding crisis and potential need for exceptional borrowing or service consolidation.
findings.figures: Current burial capacity: 10 years at 20 plots/year; with investment, 16 years. Cremation capacity: 4 years at 15 plots/year; with investment, 30 years. Special Expenses working balance: current £50k, proposed £100k target.
findings.quote: Work is progressing to maximise capacity at the existing Thorpe Road Cemetery to increase its longevity for both burial and cremation space. The current capacity for burial plots remaining based on an average of 20 plots purchased per year is 10 years, and through some investment already set aside for the cemetery, further additional capacity of 6 years can be provided.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Financial Resilience Index shows Melton at higher risk than peer authorities due to level and use of reserves; audit system nationally has collapsed with S114 reports being issued.
findings.detail: CIPFA's Financial Resilience Index rates Melton as higher risk compared to nearest neighbours (most comparable authorities) and all district councils due to lower reserves relative to net revenue expenditure. The council has also increased reliance on fees and charges income (now rated high risk), which is volatile during downturns. The report notes that audit system nationally has "collapsed" with many councils receiving disclaimed opinions; several S114 reports issued by s151 officers indicating councils in financial difficulty, including some that have not behaved imprudently but are struggling with financial pressures.
findings.matters: A lender uses external audit and financial resilience indices to assess council financial health. Melton's index position relative to peers signals above-average risk. National context of council failures and audit delays adds systemic risk.
findings.figures: CIPFA Financial Resilience Index shows higher risk vs. nearest neighbours and all district councils. Reserves improved since 2023/24 but remain below comparable authorities.
findings.quote: The Council is deemed at higher risk compared to its nearest neighbours (most comparable authorities) and all district Councils due to its level and use of reserves in comparison to net revenue expenditure. This has improved since 2023/24 with the increases in the reserves but the council still has lower reserves compared to similar authorities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Homelessness costs are rising and forecast to overspend; growth proposal adds £51,500 ongoing for increased staffing but reflects rising demand across the country.
findings.detail: 2025/26 shows forecast overspends in bed & breakfast accommodation (£28k), rent deposit scheme (£39k), with only partial offset from asylum dispersal grant and homelessness topup grant. The budget includes £51,500 recurring growth to make temporary staffing changes permanent and increase Housing Options Officer capacity, reflecting "rising demand pressures which are reflective of an increasing challenge in this area across the country". Risk assessment rates homelessness as High/Critical: "Homelessness costs are unable to be contained within budget as a result of rising need and complexity of cases."
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need to track demand-led cost pressures that may not be controllable. Homelessness is cyclical with economic conditions and requires ongoing revenue funding.
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast overspends: bed & breakfast £28k, rent deposit scheme £39k. Growth proposal: £51,500 recurring. Risk rating: High/Critical.
findings.quote: This supports the team to ensure they can meet existing and rising demand pressures which are reflective of an increasing challenge in this area across the country.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) transition costs of £250k+ in 2026/27, with further resources likely needed in future years; timing still uncertain and risk of delay exacerbating financial position.
findings.detail: The council must fund LGR transition from existing revenue budgets. £250k is set aside for initial work in 2026/27, with the S151 Officer stating "it is likely further resources will need to be deployed for this purpose in future years". LGR vesting day timing is not yet confirmed, creating planning uncertainty. The report explicitly notes: "Should vesting day for the new unitary councils be confirmed as April 2028, this will mitigate some of the financial risks the council is facing. Delay in LGR will exacerbate them and increase the need for more decisive action."
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that transformation costs are uncertain in quantum and timing, and that delay in the reorganisation directly worsens the council's medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £250k delegated to Cabinet to access Corporate Priorities Reserve for LGR transition in 2026/27. Report notes "further resources will be required subsequently" but does not quantify.
findings.quote: Recognising the imperative to invest in and fund LGR transition, delegate authority to the Cabinet to access the Corporate Priorities Reserve for up to £250k to fund any initial transition costs, recognising further resources may be required subsequently.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Capital resources are almost exhausted and cannot support asset maintenance backlog; future asset repairs risk becoming unaffordable.
findings.detail: The council's capital receipts are "almost exhausted" with pressure exacerbated by having to fund food waste vehicles from capital in 2025/26. Condition surveys on corporate assets have identified maintenance needs, but the council is currently undertaking "only essential asset repairs as a result of affordability". Risk assessment identifies this as Very High/Critical: if deferred maintenance accumulates, future repair costs may become unaffordable. Examples include Phoenix House (£63k service charge adjustment), Asfordby Road embankment requiring £74k clearance for inspection access, and corporate condition surveys now required.
findings.matters: A lender assesses an authority's asset base and maintenance risk. Depleted capital receipts and deferred maintenance signal risk of future borrowing need or asset deterioration affecting service delivery.
findings.figures: Corporate Repairs and Maintenance growth proposals: £77,500 condition surveys, £74,000 Asfordby Road embankment clearance. Phoenix House prior year service charge adjustment £63,000. Special Expenses: £13,120 repairs + £16,250 condition surveys.
findings.quote: Capital resources are almost exhausted, with pressure exacerbated by the need to meet the shortfall in capital funding from Central Government to purchase food waste vehicles in 25/26. They have been supplemented in recent years by a number of disposals.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Business rates reset and pool dissolution removes £257k+ of previously available funding; council is one of circa 67 most-affected authorities nationally under new formula.
findings.detail: The finance settlement includes a business rates reset, removal of all previous growth, and dissolution of the Leicester and Leicestershire business rates pool. Council previously benefited from pool redistributions and successful bids for projects. The new funding formula particularly disadvantages shire districts (sparsity removed as factor), placing Melton in the most-affected 67 councils nationally. The council receives only 95% transitional protection in 2027/28 and 2028/29, meaning real-terms funding cuts. Core spending power remains static in cash terms while inflation continues.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that a major revenue source has been removed permanently through government policy change, and the council is formally disputing this with MHCLG as "disproportionately negative". This is structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: Business rates equalisation reserve: £487k balance 1.4.26, drawn down by £323k to £164k by 31.3.27. Core spending power: £9.2m 2026/27, flat to 2028/29, then drops to £9.2m 2029/30. Transitional protection at 95% of adjusted 2025/26 funding in 2027/28 and 2028/29.
findings.quote: The finance settlement has fundamentally changed this position and created disproportionate winners and losers. The negative and presumably unintended impact of the finance settlement has been raised directly with the Secretary of State and senior MHCLG officials and discussions are ongoing as part of and subsequent to the Government's consultation to establish whether any mitigation of this impact is possible.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27 and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Food waste collection costs of £779k+ per year cannot be afforded without significant service reductions or government exemption.
findings.detail: The government promised full funding for food waste collections under the New Burdens Doctrine but has not delivered it transparently. The council has insufficient funding to implement the scheme as required by April 2026 and is formally requesting a delay until April 2028 post-LGR. Without this delay, implementing food waste would "significantly increase the deficit" and potentially place the council in an "unsustainable position". The council has written to the Secretary of State and DEFRA escalating this.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to know whether the council can fund a £800k+ annual service demand, and whether the government will force implementation or grant relief. This is the single largest financial pressure in the report.
findings.figures: £779,380 + £112,370 annual vehicle replacement cost for full roll out; partial year 2026/27 cost estimated at lesser amount; vehicles delivery delayed to latter part of 2026
findings.quote: Due to supply chain pressures delaying the delivery of food waste vehicles until the latter part of 2026, coupled with the funding uncertainties and therefore a delayed renegotiation and variation of the waste collection contract, the earliest food waste collections could be implemented would be January 2027, meaning (if implemented) a lesser (partial year) cost pressure would arise in 2026/27. Nevertheless, the ongoing full year cost impact on the Council's budget would be significant and very quickly become unsustainable and potentially place the council in a financially unsustainable position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: HRA carrying £31.5m debt with no repayment plan, relying on cash accumulation instead
findings.detail: The HRA business plan, approved in 2022/23, makes no provision for debt repayment on either existing or new borrowing. Under HRA self-financing, the council has opted to build cash reserves rather than pay down the £31.5m debt balance. New HRA borrowing affordability will be assessed using industry standard indicators, but the council is comfortable carrying the debt without repayment.
findings.matters: A housing authority deferring all debt repayment indefinitely increases leverage and relies entirely on cash generation to manage liquidity; it also means any rent pressures directly threaten the financial model.
findings.figures: HRA borrowing £31,484k in 2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29 (flat across all years)
findings.quote: The HRA business plan, approved in 2022/23, provides for no provision for the repayment of debt for either existing or new debt. However, where new unsupported borrowing is undertaken for the HRA the affordability of new borrowing will be assessed, tracked and monitored using industry standard indicators to ensure interest payments are affordable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Property fund has fallen to £1.841m from £2m investment, with statutory protection for losses expiring in 2029
findings.detail: The council invested £2m in a CCLA property fund, now valued at £1.841m as of 31 December 2025 (a loss of £159k from September 2025). A reserve has been established to absorb potential further losses. However, a statutory override protecting revenue from losses expires on 31 March 2029, after which any remaining deficit would be charged directly to the revenue account. The risk register rates property fund valuation loss as Medium Risk.
findings.matters: A council with an underwater investment that could force a revenue charge in three years is material to lending decisions, especially if the reserve is depleted before the override expires.
findings.figures: £2m initial investment; current valuation £1.841m; notional loss £159k from September 2025; reserve expected to be £190k at end of 2025/26; statutory override until 31 March 2029
findings.quote: Due to the risks associated with this type of investment, the Council has established a reserve to help offset any potential deficits that may arise. A statutory override is currently in place, which has been extended to 31st March 2029, meaning that any future gains or losses from then onwards must be credited or charged to the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme 2026-2030 - General Fund and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Stockyard Levelling Up Fund project (£11.4m+) moving into construction July 2026 after government deadline extension and design completion.
findings.detail: The council's largest capital commitment, the Stockyard worth £11.4m total, has been reprofiled following government timeframe extension to March 2028. Planning consent was granted February 2025, design review completed December 2025, and main construction works are expected to start July 2026. £1.9m is planned for 2026/27.
findings.matters: This is the council's dominant capital project. A lender should track its progress as it moves into the construction phase and monitor cost and timeline developments.
findings.figures: £11.4m total project; £1.9m budgeted 2026/27; delivery deadline March 2028; construction start July 2026
findings.quote: The Stockyard (LUF) programme has been reprofiled in line with current forecasts and project delivery plans. The government has extended the timeframe for delivery to March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme 2026-2030 - General Fund and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Borrowing planned for 2028/29 to fund Levelling Up Fund project continuation.
findings.detail: Although no borrowing is required in 2026/27, the five-year capital forecast indicates borrowing will be needed from 2028/29 onwards to fund the remainder of the Stockyard Levelling Up Fund project. This borrowing has already been approved.
findings.matters: A lender should understand the council's planned debt trajectory. Capital spending will require borrowing within three years, adding to revenue budget pressures.
findings.figures: No borrowing 2026/27; borrowing likely 2028/29
findings.quote: The forecast 5-year programme indicates borrowing will be likely in 2028/29 as already approved for the LUF project.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme 2026-2030 - General Fund and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Corporate Priorities Reserve already under pressure from revenue commitments, constraining capital spending options.
findings.detail: The revenue reserve used to support capital spending is already heavily drawn to meet forecast revenue commitments. This forces capital schemes to compete for limited funding and means any additional capital investment will likely require borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council has limited capital funding headroom. Revenue pressures directly constrain capital investment choices and signal future debt will be required.
findings.figures: Corporate Priorities Reserve under pressure; capital receipts expected to be exhausted
findings.quote: This revenue reserve is already under pressure in order to meet forecast revenue commitments Therefore, the prioritisation of capital schemes is important

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme 2026-2030 - General Fund and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Lake Terrace surface water drainage: new £260k capital commitment with acknowledged high risk, only at design stage.
findings.detail: The council is committing £260k to surface water drainage works at the council-owned Lake Terrace site, described as a complex and longstanding issue only at RIBA Stage 2 design. The Property and Assets Programme Board is overseeing it due to recognised high risk.
findings.matters: A lender should track this new high-risk capital commitment as it progresses from early design through delivery, noting the acknowledged complexity.
findings.figures: £260k new capital commitment; RIBA Stage 2 design only
findings.quote: the project carries a high degree of risk and will be overseen through the Property and Assets Programme Board

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Programme 2026-2030 - General Fund and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Asset Development Programme has forced professional services costs to revenue, reducing available capital receipts.
findings.detail: The ADP project incurred capital costs that could not be capitalized and were charged to revenue instead. This directly reduces capital receipts available for future schemes. The risk register identifies this as Critical impact with Significant likelihood.
findings.matters: A lender must understand actual capital funding capacity. Revenue-charging of capital costs reduces the council's ability to self-fund future capital investment without borrowing.
findings.figures: Risk marked Significant likelihood / Critical impact
findings.quote: ADP capital spend to date has to be charged to revenue due to no capital expenditure having been incurred and therefore capital receipts funding can't be used.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Structural works invoice of £46k completed in 2024/25 not accrued, extrapolating to £77.5k potential error.
findings.detail: Auditor identified that an invoice dated 25 March 2025 for £46k (£38k net) for structural works completed in 2024/25 was not accrued in the financial statements. Due to testing scope, extrapolation suggests a maximum potential error of £77.5k, which exceeds the trivial reporting threshold. The Authority did not adjust despite the amount exceeding trivial threshold.
findings.matters: Accrual principle is fundamental to accurate financial position. A council not accruing for work completed suggests expenditure may be understated and commitments not fully captured.
findings.figures: £46k invoice not accrued; £77.5k extrapolated maximum error
findings.quote: The Authority did not accrue for an invoice received after year end dated 25.3.25 for structural works completed in 2024/25 totalling £46k (£38k net of VAT)... the potential maximum error would be extrapolated to £77.5k which is above our trivial level for reporting.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Payables balance overstated by £431k due to incorrect classification of prepayments.
findings.detail: Auditor testing identified that the payables balance included £431k of debit balances relating to prepayments, which should be shown in receivables under CIPFA Code. This was corrected as an adjusted misstatement. Auditor noted extrapolation suggests a further potential maximum error of £192k elsewhere in payables, though not material enough to adjust.
findings.matters: Classification errors affect the shape of the balance sheet and can mask real payment obligations. The auditor's note of further potential errors suggests the classification control needs strengthening.
findings.figures: £431k adjusted; £192k potential maximum additional error identified
findings.quote: The payables balance, which is a credit balance recorded on the balance sheet, included debit balances relating to prepayments... resulted in the payables balance was understated by £431k with a corresponding understatement of the receivables balance of £431k.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Old debts of £227k over 5 years old, with only £218k provided for, creating collection risk.
findings.detail: Auditor identified £227k of receivables over 5 years old with only £218k provision made. The age of debt directly impacts collectability and receipt of this income. This issue was also raised in the prior year, indicating it has not been resolved.
findings.matters: A lender assessing cash flow sustainability needs to know how much historic debt is uncollectable. Stale debt represents income that is unlikely to materialise and affects usable reserves.
findings.figures: £227k total old debts over 5 years; £218k provided; £9k unprovisioned
findings.quote: Currently debt over 5 years old totals £227k of which the Authority has provided for £218k. The age of this debt will impact its collectability and subsequent receipt of this income.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Finance leases (refuse vehicles from 2018) were not disclosed in prior years, now recognised as £954k asset and £1,081k liability.
findings.detail: IFRS 16 implementation revealed leases for refuse vehicles taken out in 2018 for ten years were previously undisclosed finance leases. These now require a prior period adjustment adding £954k to property plant and equipment and £1,081k to lease liabilities, with £127k adjustment to unusable reserves. This indicates controls over lease identification have been weak.
findings.matters: This represents material liabilities and assets omitted from prior-year statements. It demonstrates the council did not have complete lease records, raising questions about what else might be unaccounted for in capital commitments.
findings.figures: £954k PPE increase, £1,081k lease liability increase, £127k reserves adjustment; 10-year lease from 2018
findings.quote: These leases for refuse vehicles taken out in 2018 for a ten year period... meet the criteria to be included on the Authority's balance sheet as a right of use asset with a related lease liability in 2024/25. As these leases relate back to 2018 this also requires a prior period adjustment as the amount is material.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council dwellings estate (Burnaby Place, Ashfordby) is not registered at land registry, creating legal ownership risk.
findings.detail: Testing of council dwellings rights and obligations identified that the entire Burnaby Place estate has not been registered with land registry. The auditor completed alternative procedures to confirm ownership rights, but notes that not registering assets appropriately creates risk around legal ownership and difficulties with future sales of these dwellings.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs assurance that council assets are properly secured legally. Unregistered property creates future encumbrance issues and could affect borrowing security or asset sales.
findings.figures: Burnaby Place, Ashfordby estate; part of £121.4m council dwellings portfolio
findings.quote: Not registering the Authority's assets appropriately could create a risk around legal ownership and in particular difficulties associated with future sales of these dwellings.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Property valuations contained material errors totalling £2.8m across formula, area calculations, and rate application.
findings.detail: Auditor testing of land and building valuations identified four material/significant errors: formula errors excluding external works caused £902k understatement; incorrect Gross Internal Areas (GIA) caused £1,911k understatement; wrong BCIS rate applied caused £127k overstatement; investment property formula error caused £234k understatement. Additionally, timing of BCIS rates could mean £72k further understatement.
findings.matters: Melton's property portfolio (£48.5m land/buildings + £121.4m council dwellings + £2.3m investment property) is 62% of total assets. Multiple calculation errors indicate control weaknesses in the valuation process with a new external valuer.
findings.figures: £902k, £1,911k, £127k, £234k, £72k errors; total property portfolio £172.2m (land/buildings £48.48m, council dwellings £121.424m, investment property £2.347m)
findings.quote: Our testing of a sample of land and building valuations identified 3 assets where supporting calculations incorrectly excluded external works due to a formula error... valuations were understated by £902k... a number of discrepancies between the Gross Internal Area (GIA) used by the valuer... resulted in valuations being understated by £1,911k.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditor issued disclaimer opinion due to no assurance over opening balances from prior year backstop.
findings.detail: The auditor cannot form an opinion on the financial statements because they have no assurance over opening balances for 2024/25. This follows a prior-year disclaimer opinion under backstop legislation. The auditor is unable to conclude whether other information published with the statements (Annual Governance Statement, narrative report) is consistent with the financial statements.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion means the auditor cannot verify the starting position for this year's accounts. Any lender relying on audited financials should understand the full audit trail is not assured.
findings.figures: 2024/25 opening balances - no assurance provided
findings.quote: The limitations imposed by not having assurance on opening balances mean that we will be unable to form an opinion on the financial statements. Our anticipated financial statements audit report opinion will be a disclaimer opinion.

news_drafts.lead: S106 contributions are a material income stream for councils and represent contractual obligations. A comprehensive process overhaul indicates the prior arrangement had issues requiring external intervention that could affect income certainty or legal…

news_drafts.lead: A major capital project operating without internal audit assurance creates governance and control risk. Lenders need confidence that significant capital schemes have been properly audited and that project controls are operating effectively.

news_drafts.headline: Monthly bank reconciliation control lapsed due to staffing vacancy and turnover in the finance team
news_drafts.lead: Staffing instability in the finance team creates risk of control lapses and suggests the team may be under-resourced for its current workload, which could affect the timeliness and reliability of financial reporting.
